problem_data.story:
THE SCENT OF DIGITAL PAINT
BY HANNAH MUNOZ

The gallery district of Maplewood, Veldoria had to be safe enough. I couldn't have been more certain. In the window of the electronics store, a holographic display was cycling through NFT art pieces, and folded in my pocket was the news article about the catastrophic failure of the new blockchain-based conservation tracking system. The young people on the corner seemed barely recognizable, hunched figures in synthetic fiber coats. It was my own time. Anyone could see I was safe, and I could risk doing what I desperately wanted to do.

I turned the corner.

The odds were against me from the start. It didn't come as any surprise. I could never get away with it. I knew that all along.

There was a Tesla parked just beyond the charging station.

The metal and glass fronts of the buildings didn't show back here, only weathered brick held together with crumbling mortar. The line of the block seemed to stretch back, ever further away from the sleek fronts into the decaying stone.

A woman brushed past me, wearing a smart blazer and carrying a tablet. And, reassuringly, she was in a hurry.

I decided to chance it. I certainly wanted to do it in the worst way.

My footsteps carried me on down the block.

A small vehicle whirred past me. One of those autonomous pods, I decided. Only it wasn't quite right. I fixed the silhouette in my mind's eye and tried to identify it. Something from the early 2020s.

Still, I wasn't worried. It was actually too early in the day. It wasn't as if it were evening or anything like that.

The little shop was right where I left it, quietly deteriorating by itself. The sign above the door had faded badly—the first word was completely illegible, weathered to nothing but gray smudges. I could only make out "...Gallery" in what had once been silver lettering against blue. In the window, in protective cases, were prints from the first digital art exhibition, a recent magazine featuring contemporary VR installations, a coffee table book about the Restoration Movement murals, and a brand-new, sun-faded catalog of the Morningside Province Ecosystem Art Project.

Next door, a newer establishment called "The Ecosystem Gallery" had opened since my last visit—all sleek glass and modern signage, advertising VR immersion experiences. But I had no interest in that place. My shop was the old one, the dying one.

There was a delivery drone at the curb. This time I recognized it was from an earlier generation.

I went in, the chrome handle making me conscious of the sweat on my palm.

The old woman sat behind a fortress of art books and magazines, treacherously scrolling through something on an ancient tablet. Her gray hair was pulled back from the sharp angles of her cardigan. She smiled, showing yellowed teeth.

"Came back for more of the work, did you? Welcome back to the Retrospective."

She set down the tablet. (That headline couldn't really be making such an accusation about the Conservation Council, could it?)

"Yes," I laughed, not very convincingly.

"I know what a craving can be. I shouldn't eat sweets, but I do. I've tried to stop but I lie there thinking about chocolate half the night. Dark chocolate, milk chocolate, truffles, plain bars. I feel like I could eat a whole box. Is it like that with you?"

"Not that bad. To me it's just—"

"Don't tell me art isn't a craving with some of you people. I've seen folks come in here, hardly two coins to rub together, and grab up those restoration journals and read and read, until sweat starts rolling off the end of their nose. I've hardly got the heart to throw them out. Not like that flashy ecosystem place next door—they'd charge you just to breathe their filtered air."

Restoration journals. Ones with beautiful landscapes being returned to their natural state, with ecosystems being rebuilt from nothing. Yes, they were a part of it. Not a big part, but a part.

"That's not what I want to see. I want—"

The old woman chuckled. "I know what you want. Indeed I do. This way."

I followed her pointing hand and sure enough, there they were. Stacks upon stacks of old art magazines from the Restoration Movement.

"Twenty credits for ones in good condition," the old woman pronounced the ritual, "ten credits for ones with damaged covers, three for twenty-five, check them at the desk when you go."

I ran my hand down a stack. *Art & Ecology*, *The Restoration Artist*, *Biodiversity Canvas*, *Creative Conservation*, all of them.

The old woman was watching me. She scuttled back across the floor and snatched up a magazine. It was a copy of *Ecosystem Visions* with a woman in paint-splattered overalls standing before a massive mural of a restored wetland.

"This one, this one," she said. "This must be a good one. I bet she painted every species that came back. Every single one. Species."

"I'll take it."

Reluctantly she handed over the magazine, waited a moment, then left me.

I stared at the stacks of Restoration Movement magazines and I felt the slow run of the drop of sweat down my nose.

My sickness was terrible. It is as bad to be nostalgic for things you have never known as for an orphan who has never had a home to be homesick.

Living in the past, that was always me. I never watched anything on the screens made later than 2025. I was fascinated by the early digital artists, the first VR creators, the pioneers of blockchain art. My favorite artists were the ones who had painted the great restoration murals in Redwood Territory.

The music I listened to was from the Cultural Exchange Movement and the early days of computational composition.

And my viewing was the documentation of the Restoration Movement, harking back to when they had first begun rebuilding the ecosystems. This was the biggest part of it all, I think.

You identify with the subject of any documentary if it's well enough made. But the identification I felt with the artists in restoration documentation was plainly ridiculous.

I was there.

I was standing before the canvas, feeling on my face the bite of the wind from the restored prairie. I was lifting my brush to capture the return of the native grasses in the dawn light. Then in a moment my hand was moving across the canvas in answer to the landscape, creating through the systematic observation that had been drilled into us, recording the biodiversity that was slowly, miraculously returning. And back through the field notes in the pocket at my knee.

Here it comes, the morning light hitting the wetland in perfect illumination. Look at that careful documentation. You can almost see the species checklist in the artist's other hand. They can afford to be methodical with that funding. I'd like to trade this rushed commission for it. That may be just what happens too if I don't watch it.

You aren't any master restorer, friend, but this is from the Maplewood Collective for the Redwood Project.

Missed that detail!

Careful with that brushstroke! God, look at the way that color bleeds. At least it was a lie about them using cheap materials.

One of your own techniques for you, amateur. Up with the palette, up under that canopy, into the shadow detail. Where am I? Where am I?

Right here.

Look at that background go. The supplier can't be giving you as good paint as they claim.

So long. I'm nodding, see.

She's pushing through. No more paint and she's pushing through. She's a good artist. Come on. A little more. A little more and you can finish it. Come on, friend. You're doing it. You're pushing through—

But not enough.

God, what a mess.

I'm sick.

That damned synthetic medium in the mix. I'll be in the bathroom until morning...

No, the air wasn't one of synthetic medium but the pleasant smell of aged paper and printer's ink.

I'd been daydreaming again. I shouldn't forget things were getting different lately. It was becoming dangerous.

I gathered up an armload of Restoration Movement magazines at random.

Leaning across the table, I noticed the curtain in back for the first time. It was a beaded curtain of many different colors, like something from an old bohemian studio. Behind the curtain was a screen. It was a comforting anti-anachronism here.

The large flat display was showing an old documentary. A very old documentary. Early footage from the first ecosystem restoration project as scientists worked to bring back a destroyed forest, standing them off from encroaching development. The flickering images caught my unblinking eyes.

A developer is sneaking across the property line, a contract in his briefcase. A young activist makes a try to stop the bulldozers, but the security forces remove her. Now a government official is arriving with the preservation order. The developer makes a try with legal action, the activists celebrate, and the official signs the protection into law. It goes through, all the way through.

The young woman is running toward the official as he finishes with the paperwork and stands, her shirt torn from the earlier struggle. The developer stands up in defeat. The official smiles. No, no, say the woman's lips. "No!" "No!" says the subtitle. The official hesitates. Swimming in bureaucracy, the developer smiles sadly and walks away.

I had seen documentaries like that before.

When I was younger, I had seen *Heritage Flashbacks* between episodes of nature shows and environmental programs. I looked at old footage and heard voices making commentary. But hadn't I also seen these images with the sound of actual field recordings and low conversation?

I had seen these images before the Collapse.

The Collapse had made a lot of difference in my life.

Art supplies were rationed, from full sets to basic kits, and prices had gone up to where you had to pay hundreds for proper materials, so high that people said the Council should do something about it.

The Restoration Movement had transformed, and artists worked on rebuilding ecosystems in both physical and digital space. Only, hadn't they also worked on the social contract, on justice theory, on ethical decision-making about what should be restored and how?

And at the community center I had participated in decision-making processes about local projects. I never did get enough votes to lead a project, but my mentor had taken my designs and incorporated parts of them for the wetland restoration. I could never get enough recognition...

"Nobody would look at my magazines," the old woman chuckled, "if I put it out front. My daughter got me that screen. She runs a digital art studio. A good girl. Her name's on the business registry."

I pressed some credits on her and walked myself out of the store. Shutting the door, I glanced at the neighboring storefronts. The sleek Ecosystem Gallery next door was doing brisk business—a crowd of young people lined up for some VR experience. But the receipt in my hand read clearly: "The Retrospective Gallery - Vintage Art Publications." Above me, the old woman's faded sign still proclaimed only "...Gallery" to anyone who didn't know its full name.

The catalog of the Ecosystem Art Project had been replaced in the window by something about the Cultural Exchange Movement.

The street was full of autonomous vehicles, sleek electric cars, boxy delivery drones, swept-back courier bikes. Only one dark, heavy, combustion-engine vehicle moved through the traffic. It had a light on the roof.

I dodged in front of a recycling truck and behind an electric postal van and ran for that light, leaving a trail of gaudy restoration images checkering the street behind me.

I grabbed the handle on the door, opened it and threw myself into the back seat.

"Central District," I said from my diaphragm, without any breath behind it.

Something was wrong. Two people were in the front seat. The driver showed me his hard, expressionless face. "What do you think you are doing?"

"This isn't a rideshare?" I asked blankly.

"Environmental Police."

I sat there while we drove on for a few minutes.

"Disoriented and disturbed," the second person said to the driver.

"Right into our laps."

The second officer leaned forward and clicked something. "I'll get the City units."

"No, kill it, Hannah. Think of all that damned paperwork."

Hannah shrugged. "What will we do with him?"

I was beginning to attach myself to my surroundings. The street was full of traffic. My kind of traffic. Vehicles that were too new or too old.

"Look, officers, I'm not disoriented or disturbed. I thought this was a rideshare. I just wanted to get away from back then—I mean back *there*."

The two officers exchanged glances.

"What were you running from?" the driver asked.

How could I tell him that?

Before I even got a chance to try, he said: "What did you do?"

"I didn't *do* anything!"

The vehicle was turning, turning into shadows, stopping. We were in an alley. Soggy cardboard, discarded containers, prowling rats, a broken die, half a dice, looking big in the frame of my thick, probably bulletproof window.

The officers opened their doors and then mine.

"Out."

I climbed out and stood by the vehicle, blinking.

"You were causing some kind of trouble in that neighborhood back there," the driver announced.

"Really, officers—"

"What's your name?"

"Noah Nguyen. There—"

"We don't want you going back there again, Nguyen, causing trouble. Understand?"

"Officer, I only bought some magazines—I mean art journals."

"These?" the second person, Hannah, asked. She had retrieved them from the back seat. "Look here, Stephen. They look pretty subversive."

Stephen took up the *Ecosystem Visions* with the woman in the paint-splattered overalls. "Dangerous," he said.

"You know about the laws governing unauthorized restoration documentation, Nguyen."

"Those aren't unauthorized and they are my property!"

I reached for them and Hannah pulled them back, grinning. "You don't want to read these. They aren't good for you. We're confiscating them."

"Look here, I'm a citizen! You can't—"

Hannah shoved me back a little. "Can't we?"

Stephen stepped in front of me, his face in deadly earnest. "How about it, Nguyen? You a memory addict?"

He grabbed my wrist and started checking my pulse, looking for signs of neural interface abuse. I twisted away from him.

"Resisting an officer," Stephen said almost sadly.

At that, Hannah moved up beside him.

The two of them started to beat me.

They hit clean, in the belly and ribs, but not in the groin. They gave me clean white flashes of pain, instead of angry, red-streaked ones. I didn't fight back, not against the two of them. I knew that much. I didn't even try to block their blows. I stood with my arms at my sides, leaning back against the vehicle, and hearing myself grunt at each blow.

They stood away from me and let me fold helplessly to the greasy pavement.

"Stay away from that neighborhood and stay out of trouble," Stephen's voice said above me.

I looked up a little bit and saw an ugly, scarred hand thumbing across a stack of half a dozen magazines like a giant deck of cards.

"Why don't you take up contemporary art?" he asked me.

I never heard the vehicle drive away.

Home. I activated the living room lights from the door, looked around for intruders for the first time I could remember, and went inside.

I threw myself on the couch and rubbed my stomach. I wasn't hurt badly. My middle was going to be sorer in the morning than it was now.

Lighting up a vape, I watched the shapes of vapor and tried to think.

I looked at it objectively, forward and back.

The solution was obvious.

First of all, I positively could *not* have been a restoration artist in the early Restoration Movement. I was in my mid-twenties; anybody could tell that by looking at me. The time was the late 2050s; anybody could tell that from the neural interface ports in the corner, the new autonomous vehicles on the street. Memories of painting restoration murals and documenting returning biodiversity stirred in me by old magazines, archived documentaries, and re-runs of *The Restoration* on the streams were mere hallucinations.

Neither could I remember attending the first Cultural Exchange festivals, hearing the debates about the social contract in the post-Collapse world, or paying a month's credits to get into the original Ecosystem Art Project exhibition.

Only... I probably had seen the Project. Hadn't I gone with my mentor to a preview? Didn't she pay reduced admission for me? So how could I remember taking a partner, dark-haired, green jacket, Zoe, and paying full price each? I couldn't. Different exhibitions. That was it. The thing had toured half a dozen times. But would it have been that expensive no more than ten years ago?

I activated a new vape cartridge.

The thing I must remember, I told myself, was that my recollections were false and unreliable. It would do me no good to keep following these false memories in a closed curve.

I touched my navel area and flinched. The beating, I was confident, had been real. But it had been a nightmare. Those officers couldn't have been true. They were a small person's bad dream about symbolized authority. They were keeping me from re-entering the past where I belonged, punishing me to make me stay in my trap of the present.

Oh, God.

I rolled over on my face and pushed it into the upholstery.

That was the worst part of it. False memories, feelings of persecution, that was one thing. Believing that you are actively caught up in a mixture of the past with the present, a surreal viscosity of reality, was something else.

I needed help.

Or if there was no help for me, it was my duty to have myself placed where I couldn't harm other citizens.

If there was one thing that working for the Conservation Council had taught me, it was social responsibility.

I took up the directory and located several memory specialists. I selected one at random, for no particular reason.

Dr. Christopher Fernandez.

I memorized the address and heaved myself to my feet.

The doctor's office was as white as the inside of a sterile laboratory.

The cool, efficient receptionist told me to wait and I did, tasting nothing inside my mouth.

After several long, peaceful minutes the inner door opened.

"Mr. Nguyen, I can't seem to find any record of an appointment for you in Dr. Fernandez's files," the man said.

I got to my feet. "Then I'll come back."

He took my arm. "No, no, I can fit you in."

"I didn't have an appointment. I just came."

"I understand."

"Maybe I had better go."

"I won't hear of it."

I could have pulled loose from him, but somehow I felt that if I did try to pull away, the grip would tighten and I would never get away.

I looked up into that long, hard, blank face that seemed so recently familiar.

"I'm Dr. Santos," he said. "I'm taking care of Dr. Fernandez's practice for him while he is on leave."

I nodded. What I was thinking could only be another symptom of my illness.

He led me inside and closed the door.

The door made a strange sound in closing. It didn't go *snick-bonk*; it made a noise like *click-clack-clunk*.

"Now," he said, "would you like to lie down on the couch and tell me about it? Some people have preconceived ideas that I don't want to fight with at the beginning. Or, if you prefer, you can sit there in front of my desk and tell me all about it. Remember, I'm a neurologist, a doctor, not just a therapist."

I took possession of the chair and Santos faced me across his desk.

"I feel," I said, "that I am caught up in some kind of temporal displacement."

"I see. Have you consumed much restoration documentation, Mr. Nguyen?"

"Some. I view a lot. All kinds of content. Historical archives, contemporary streams, educational programs, entertainment feeds."

"You should *view* them instead of live them. Catharsis. Sublimate, Mr. Nguyen. For instance, to a certain type of person, I often recommend contemporary action feeds."

I seemed to be losing control of the conversation. "But this temporal displacement..."

"Mr. Nguyen, do you really believe in 'temporal displacement'?"

"No."

"Then how can there be any such thing? It can't be real."

"I know that! I want to be cured of imagining it."

"The first step is to utterly renounce the idea. Stop thinking about the past. Think of the future."

"How did you know I keep slipping back into the past?" I asked.

Santos's hands were more expressive than his face. "You mentioned temporal displacement..."

"But not to the past or to the future," I said.

"But you did, Mr. Nguyen. You told me all about thinking you could go into the past by visiting a gallery where they sold old magazines. You told me how the intrusion of the past got worse with every visit."

I blinked. "I did? I did?"

"Of course."

I stood up. "I did not!"

"Please try to keep from getting violent, Mr. Nguyen. People like you actually have more control over themselves than you realize. If you *will* yourself to be calm..."

"I *know* I didn't tell you a thing about any gallery. I'm starting to think I'm not sick at all. You—you're trying to do something to me. You're all in it together."

Santos shook his head sadly.

I realized how it all sounded.

"Good—GOD!" I moaned.

I put my hands to my face and I felt the vein over my left eye swelling, pulsing.

Through the bars of my fingers I saw Santos motion me down with one eloquent hand. I took my hands away—I didn't like looking through bars—and sat down.

"Now," Santos said, steepling his fingers, "I know of a completely appropriate facility in Crestwood. Of course, if you respond properly..."

Those hands of his.

There was something about them that wasn't right. They might have been the hands of a corpse, or a synthetic...

I lurched across the desk and grabbed his wrist.

"*Please*, Mr. Nguyen! Violence will—"

My fingers clawed at the backs of his hands and my nails dragged off ugly strips of some theatrical material—synthetic skin, I think—that had covered the scrapes and bruises he had taken hammering away at me and my belt buckle.

Santos.

Stephen.

I let go of him and stood away.

For the first time, Santos smiled.

I backed to the door and turned the handle behind my back. It wouldn't open.

I turned around and rattled it, pulled on it, braced my foot against the wall and tugged.

"Locked," Santos supplied.

He was coming toward me, I could tell. I wheeled and faced him. He had a neural interface device. It was the smallest one I had ever seen and it had an iridescence or luminosity about it, a gleaming silver needle.

I closed with him.

By the way he moved, I knew he was trained in physical combat, but you can't win them all, and I had been in a lot of fights when I had been younger. (Hadn't I?)

I stepped in while he was trying to decide whether to use the device on me or drop it to have his hands free. I palm-struck him in the solar plexus and crossed my fist into the hollow of the apex arch of his jawbone. He dropped.

I gave him a kick at the base of his spine. He grunted and lay still.

There was a knocking on the door. "Doctor? Doctor?"

I searched through his pockets. He didn't have any keys. He didn't have any money or identification or a weapon. He had a cloth and a stylus.

The receptionist had moved away from the door and was talking to somebody, in person or on a comm or intercom.

There wasn't any back door.

I went to the window. The city stretched out in an impressive panorama. On the street below, traffic crawled. There was a ledge. Quite a wide, old-fashioned ornamental ledge.

The ledge ran beneath the windows of all the offices on this floor. The twenty-first, I remembered.

I had seen it done in entertainment feeds all my life. Action heroes were always doing it for some reason or other. I had a good reason.

I unlatched the window and climbed out into the dry, crisp breeze.

The entertainment feeds didn't know much about physics. The updraft nearly lifted me off the ledge, but the cornice was so wide I could keep out of the wind if I kept myself flat against the side of the building.

The next window was about twenty feet away. I had covered half that distance, moving my feet with a sideways shuffle, when Hannah, indisputably the second officer, put her head out of the window where I was heading and pointed a weapon at me, saying in a let's-have-no-foolishness tone: "Get in here."

I went the other way.

The cool, efficient receptionist was in Santos's window with the tiny silver device in readiness.

I kept shuffling toward the receptionist. I had decided I would rather wrestle with her over the device than fight Hannah over the weapon. Idiotically, I smiled at that idea.

I slipped.

I was falling down the twenty-one stories without even a moment of windmilling for balance. I was just gone.

Lines were converging, and I was converging on the lines.

You aren't going to be able to recover from this fall, Nguyen. Good-by, Nguyen.

Death.

A sleep, a reawakening, a lie. It's nothing like that. It's nothing.

The end of everything you ever were or ever could be.

I hit.

My kneecap hurt terribly. I had scraped it badly.

Reality was all over me in patches. I showed through as a line drawing, crudely done, a sketch.

Some kind of projection. High-resolution hologram, that was all reality meant.

I was kneeling on a hard surface no more than six feet from the window from which I had fallen. It was still twenty-one flights up, more or less, but *Down* was broken and splattered over me.

I stood up, moving forward a step.

It brought me halfway through the projection, halfway through the wall at the base of the building. The other side of the screen. The solid side, I found, stepping through, bracing a hand on the image.

Looking up twenty-one floors, I saw an unbroken line of peacefully closed panes.

I remembered riding up in the elevator, the moments inside, the faint feeling of vertigo. Of course, who was to say the elevator really moved? Maybe they had only switched scenery on me while I was caught inside, listening to the artificial hum, seeing the flashing lights. Either alter the oxygen supply inside the cubicle suddenly or use subtle neural stimulation and that would contribute a sensation of change, of movement. They had it all worked out.

My fingers rubbed my head briskly, both hands working, trying to get some circulation in my brain.

I guessed I had to run. There didn't seem much else to do.

I ran.

Get help?

Not this elderly man and his grandson. Not this construction worker on her way to a job site. Not the accountant. Maybe the gallery owner, ex-Council, community leader, solid, respectable, well-intentioned, not a complete fool. The person on the corner checking a tablet by the transit stop.

"I need help," I panted to them. "Somebody's trying to kidnap me."

"Really makes you concerned to hear about something like that, doesn't it?" they said. "I'm in favor of stronger citizen protection laws myself."

"I'm not sure whether—"

"This heat is oppressive, isn't it? Especially here in these urban canyons. Sometimes I wish I was back in Crestwood. Cool, shaded streets..."

"Listen to me! These people, they're conspiring against me, trying to drive me insane! Two officers, a receptionist—"

"For my money, the Ecosystem Art Project is *the* achievement of our generation. I just don't understand these people who say it hasn't got merit. It gets merit by demonstrating what restoration can accomplish..."

They were like anybody you might talk to on the street. I knew what they would say if I cued them with "sports" or "politics" instead of the key words I had used.

I should have known better, but I wanted to touch them in some way, make them know I was alive. I grabbed them and shook them by the shoulders, and there was a whoosh and as I might have expected they collapsed like the insubstantiality they were.

There was a stick figure of a person left before me, an economical skeleton supporting the shell of a human being and two-thirds of a business suit.

Hide.

I went into the first shop I came to—Artisan Supplies.

Appropriately, it was a false front.

A neutral-colored gray surface, too smooth for concrete, stretched away into some shadows. The area was littered with trash.

Containers, bottles, what looked like the skin of a dehydrated human being—obviously, on second thought, only the discarded skin of one of the things like the one I had deflated.

And a moldering pile of documents and files.

Something caught my eye and I kicked through them. Yes, the proposal I had written to the Conservation Council in Redwood Territory, unopened. *And which they had approved.*

My work.

The work I had done for the Council, important, creative work. There was my design, the sketch of the wetland restoration, the families, children, elders, the caption: Biodiversity Conservation is Part of Our Social Contract.

All of it lying here to rot.

Something made me look away from that terrible trash.

Santos stood in the entrance of Artisan Supplies, something bright in his hand.

Something happened.

I had been wrong.

The shining instrument had not been a neural interface device.

"You're resilient," Santos said as I eased back into focus.

"You aren't, not without help," I told him in disgust.

"Spirited, aren't you? I meant mental resilience. That's the one thing we can never judge. I think you could have taken the shock right from the start. Of course, you would still have needed the conditioning to integrate properly."

"Conditioning? Conditioning?" It came out of me, vortexing up, outside of my control. "What have you done to my mind?"

"We've been trying to get it to grow back up," Santos said reasonably. "Think of this. Restoration. Renewal. Rejuvenation. This is it. Never mind how it works. Most minds can't stand being young and knowing they will have to go through the same experience all over again. We use neural remapping to shift your upper conscious memories to your subconscious, leaving room for new memories. You remember only those things out of the past you *have* to, to retain your identity."

"Identity," I repeated. "I have no identity. My identity is a dream. I have two identities—one of them decades beyond the other."

Santos tilted his head and his eyes at me and slapped me across the face. "Don't go back on me now. We gave you the best we could. The Rejuvenation Service couldn't help it if you were too old for a *beta*. You shouldn't have waited until you were so old, so very old. We used the very oldest sets and simulations we had for *betas*, but you, you had to keep wandering onto *alpha* territory, while they were striking sets, even. *Beta* or not, we gave you good service. Don't slip now."

I heard the voice and I heard another voice, and it said "What could you expect of a *beta*?" and they were only some of the voices I was hearing, and I wondered what you could expect from a *beta*, and I didn't know, or think that I would ever know.

The Ecosystem Gallery, with its <v_quote>sleek glass and modern signage</v_quote>, aligns with this interest. The Retrospective Gallery, in contrast, is described as <v_quote>quietly deteriorating</v_quote>, implying it's not the protagonist's main focus. By considering the protagonist's motivations and the district's atmosphere, it's clear that "The Ecosystem Gallery" is the more relevant and visited gallery, making it the correct answer.
